<reason>PRO locked the principle early (CON conceded a shrunk box is a price rise) and then converted every CON objection into "disclose nothing." The decisive moves were PRO's pressure questions: if the habit shopper reads nothing, why do firms retool moulds to keep the sticker unchanged, and if quality-shrink substitutes are free, why is pack-shrinking the dominant tactic? CON's answers ("she reads the number, not the prose"; "shrinking is only marginally cheaper") were plausible but conceded ground — and PRO's closing turned the first back on CON's own remedy (a bigger unit-price number she supposedly doesn't consult). PRO also handled the expiry question cleanly: a sticker rise is visible for one day, a flag for a year, the status quo for zero days. CON's best surviving line — uniform category-wide flags don't differentiate options — was real but underweighed against PRO's "that's how much is being hidden" plus the repeat-trip window to trade down. CON was sharp and disciplined, but its route rested on attention-scarcity and substitution claims that PRO's cost logic materially dented. Both sides had clipped turns; execution costs roughly cancel.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A3.1/A4.5 contradiction attack — manufacturers spend on new moulds precisely because the shopper reads the sticker — paired with the closing point that CON's own bigger-unit-price alternative dies first if attention is as scarce as CON claims. CON's B4.1 "number not prose" reply was the best available answer but left the tension unresolved.</best_rebuttal>
